topics.topic: Concrete representation, precision, and cross-precision comparison of backup and cutoff instants
questions: What exact representation and precision do backup-record instants and the clock-derived cutoff use, including whether precision is uniform when an instant is recorded?
What exact representation and precision must the backup record and the cutoff use, so that choosing the precision is not left to the implementer?
What concrete representation and precision do the clock reading and stored backup instant have, and how are values with different precisions compared without inventing or discarding fractional time?

quotes:
Every duration in this decision — the 8 hours, the 30, 15 and 10
   minutes, the 60 seconds — is measured by the process's monotonic clock,
   which a change of the wall clock does not move and which counts the time
   the host or its VM was suspended, so a session does not outlive a
   suspension; instants Registry records
   and the 03:00 of A18 are UTC wall-clock time.
Every time Registry records is an instant in UTC with time zone (L16).

The cutoff and
   each record's UTC instant (L16) are compared as instants at the full
   precision each holds, neither rounded nor truncated; a backup whose
   instant is earlier than the cutoff is deleted.
judgement.divergence: One implementation records and compares whole-second instants while another records and compares fractional-second instants; a backup near the 720-hour boundary is consequently deleted by one and kept by the other, which the owner notices in the kept-backup listing.
judgement.why: The texts select UTC wall-clock instants but leave their concrete representation and precision open, so the instruction to retain each value's full precision does not produce uniform boundary behavior.

witness.initial: A backup snapshot is fixed at 2026-10-12T12:00:00.400Z, and a later retention step reads its clock at 2026-11-11T12:00:00.500Z.
events: Registry records the snapshot instant in the backup's readable record.
Registry starts the third step, reads its one cutoff-source instant, subtracts exactly 720 hours, and compares the record with the cutoff.
The owner opens the interface that shows the newest kept backup.
outcomes: An implementation retaining fractional seconds compares 12:00:00.400Z with 12:00:00.500Z and deletes the backup.
An implementation whose permitted instant representation retains only whole seconds compares 12:00:00Z with 12:00:00Z and keeps the backup.
witness.observer: The owner viewing the newest kept backup.
basis:
The copy's read transaction fixes its
   snapshot by its first read, which is of the audit counter's last
   sequence number, and the instant is read from the clock at that read; a
   change committed after it is not in this backup, which holds the store as
   its snapshot saw it, and a later backup holds whatever the store holds
   when its own snapshot is fixed.

The owner interface shows the instant of the newest kept backup whose record
   can be read, or that there is none, from one listing of the backup
   location; read while a run renames or deletes, it shows the state before
   or after that change, never a temporary file.

judgement.divergence: A test implementation using only exact-second boundary cases accepts code that truncates instants, while a test using a fractional boundary rejects it; the agent judging whether the required tests prove the invariant sees different results, and the accepted truncating implementation can later keep or delete a backup differently for the owner.
judgement.why: Required test 7 distinguishes equality from a full-second difference but does not require any fractional or mixed-precision case capable of detecting rounding or truncation.

witness.initial: The implementation truncates backup and cutoff instants to whole seconds before comparison, while the required test supplies only an exactly 720-hour-old backup and one older by one full second.
events: The required test runs the two stated whole-second cases.
The truncating implementation keeps the exact-boundary backup and deletes the backup one second earlier.
A full-precision implementation runs the same required test.
outcomes: The truncating implementation passes the stated Required test despite violating the full-precision rule.
The full-precision implementation also passes, so the Required test does not demonstrate the rule against rounding or truncation.
witness.observer: The agent judging whether the Required tests prove the invariant.

topics.topic: Retention cutoff clock source and the exact instant when the cutoff is sampled
questions: Is “older than 30 × 24 hours” in the formal invariant measured against the third step's fixed starting cutoff, or against the later instant when the run finishes?
What clock measures that minute, and on what exact cadence or triggering rule must the process read it?
Which clock supplies this UTC instant, and is it the same UTC wall-clock source used for recorded backup instants?

quotes:
Every duration in this decision — the 8 hours, the 30, 15 and 10
   minutes, the 60 seconds — is measured by the process's monotonic clock,
   which a change of the wall clock does not move and which counts the time
   the host or its VM was suspended, so a session does not outlive a
   suspension; instants Registry records
   and the 03:00 of A18 are UTC wall-clock time.

The process looks at the clock at least once a minute; a date's
   run starts at its first look at or after 03:00 of that date when an
   earlier look of the same process saw that date before 03:00, and no kept
   backup of that date exists — a kept backup's date being the UTC date of
   its recorded instant, and a file whose record cannot be read counting as
   none (rule 4), so
   a restart, a start at 03:00 or a clock set back makes no second run.

Third, whatever the second step did, it deletes every kept
   backup made more than 30 × 24 hours before the instant this step starts,
   one cutoff for the whole step — a backup made exactly 30 × 24 hours before
   it is kept. The step reads the clock once, before it looks at any file,
   and its cutoff is that UTC instant less exactly 720 hours.
judgement.why: The normative rules make the formal invariant relative to the third step's single starting cutoff, identify the relevant clock as UTC wall-clock time, and define the permitted polling cadence and trigger.
